Raguva Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Raguva, Lithuania

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Raguva during the 17th century; by 1897, the Jewish population peaked at 1,223 (69% of residents), still numbering around 500 before WWII. The town's economy revolved around trade with local estate owners and two Jewish-owned factories producing leather and brushes, employing about 100 people; a 1931 census found 11 of the town's 12 businesses Jewish-owned. Jewish life centered on an 18th-century wooden synagogue with a carved Holy Ark and a large late-19th-century Beit Midrash; the Zionist-Socialist party led most cultural activity in town. This cemetery was established in the 17th century and also served Panevėžys's Jews, who had no cemetery of their own at the time. Germany occupied Raguva on June 26, 1941; by mid-August the entire community was transferred to the Panevėžys Ghetto, and on August 24 both Raguva's and Panevėžys's Jews were murdered together at Pajuoste forest - a mass grave later found by Soviet authorities to contain around 8,000 victims. In 1948, a Soviet military cemetery was established in the abandoned southeastern part of the Jewish cemetery grounds. The site was added to Lithuania's Cultural Property Register in 2015.
